claim: Oxygen isotopic compositions (δ18O) of tooth enamel are a direct method of reconstructing environmental variation experienced by an individual animal.
source: Oxygen isotopic compositions (δ18O) of tooth enamel are a direct method of reconstructing environmental variation experienced by an individual animal.
evidence: This is a general statement about the methodology that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of isotope geochemistry and paleoenvironmental reconstruction.

claim: Comparisons of δ18O values (n=2016) in twelve molars from six modern Bornean and Sumatran orangutans reveal a high degree of overlap.
source: Comparisons of δ18O values (n=2016) in twelve molars from six modern Bornean and Sumatran orangutans reveal a high degree of overlap, with more consistent annual and bimodal rainfall patterns in the Sumatran individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from 2016 measurements across 12 molars from 6 modern orangutans as stated in the abstract.

claim: Modern Bornean and Sumatran orangutans show more consistent annual and bimodal rainfall patterns in the Sumatran individuals.
source: Comparisons of δ18O values (n=2016) in twelve molars from six modern Bornean and Sumatran orangutans reveal a high degree of overlap, with more consistent annual and bimodal rainfall patterns in the Sumatran individuals.
evidence: This is based on analysis of δ18O data from modern orangutan teeth.

claim: Fossil Sumatran orangutans show similarities with modern Sumatran individuals in δ18O values.
source: Comparisons with fossil orangutan δ18O values (n=955 measurements from six molars) reveal similarities between modern and late Pleistocene fossil Sumatran individuals, but differences between modern and late Pleistocene/early Holocene Bornean orangutans.
evidence: This is based on comparison of 955 measurements from six fossil molars with modern data.

claim: Fossil Bornean orangutans show differences from modern Bornean orangutans in δ18O values.
source: Comparisons with fossil orangutan δ18O values (n=955 measurements from six molars) reveal similarities between modern and late Pleistocene fossil Sumatran individuals, but differences between modern and late Pleistocene/early Holocene Bornean orangutans.
evidence: This is based on comparison of fossil and modern δ18O data.

claim: Late Pleistocene/early Holocene northern Borneo had drier and more open environments with reduced monsoon intensity.
source: These suggest drier and more open environments with reduced monsoon intensity during this earlier period in northern Borneo, consistent with other Niah Caves studies and long-term speleothem δ18O records in the broader region.
evidence: This interpretation is based on δ18O data from fossil orangutans and is consistent with other studies cited.

claim: Present-day rainfall patterns in Indonesia are controlled by the Asian and Australian monsoon systems.
source: Present-day rainfall patterns in Indonesia are controlled by the Asian and Australian monsoon systems, yielding annual trends that vary considerably with geography, topography, and the direction of monsoonal winds (Aldrian and Dwi Susanto, 2003; Moron et al., 2009; Qian et al., 2013; Belgaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Northern Sumatra and western Borneo experience high annual rainfall and relatively stable annual temperatures.
source: Northern Sumatra and western Borneo experience high annual rainfall and relatively stable annual temperatures, with a bimodal distribution of rainfall governed by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (Van Schaik, 1986; Aldrian and Dwi Susanto, 2003; Belgaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Northern Sumatra and western Borneo have a bimodal distribution of rainfall governed by the Intertropical Convergence Zone.
source: Northern Sumatra and western Borneo experience high annual rainfall and relatively stable annual temperatures, with a bimodal distribution of rainfall governed by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (Van Schaik, 1986; Aldrian and Dwi Susanto, 2003; Belgaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sumatra and Borneo are under the influence of inter-annual climate fluctuations driven by the El-Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO).
source: These islands are also under the influence of inter-annual climate fluctuations driven by the El-Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO); a periodic coupling of atmospheric and oceanic temperature gradients that initiates in the tropical Pacific, and influences global temperature and precipitation trends (Marshall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Variation in rainfall patterns influences the fundamental structure of primate habitats.
source: It is well understood that variation in rainfall patterns influences the fundamental structure of primate habitats (Brockman and Van Schaik, 2005; Wessling et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Dense tropical forests are sustained by fairly consistent rainfall and short, irregular dry seasons.
source: Dense tropical forests are sustained by fairly consistent rainfall and short, irregular dry seasons, while woodland communities in more arid environments have smaller trees, less dense canopies, and more deciduous trees (Vico et al., 2017; Archibald et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Woodland communities in more arid environments have smaller trees, less dense canopies, and more deciduous trees.
source: Dense tropical forests are sustained by fairly consistent rainfall and short, irregular dry seasons, while woodland communities in more arid environments have smaller trees, less dense canopies, and more deciduous trees (Vico et al., 2017; Archibald et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Open woodland and savannah environments are unfavorable for slow-moving orangutans.
source: Open woodland and savannah environments are unfavorable for slow-moving orangutans, the largest mammal with an arboreal lifestyle, particularly in regions with predators such as tigers or humans (Thorpe and Crompton, 2009; Ashbury et al., 2015; Spehar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Orangutans are the largest mammal with an arboreal lifestyle.
source: Open woodland and savannah environments are unfavorable for slow-moving orangutans, the largest mammal with an arboreal lifestyle, particularly in regions with predators such as tigers or humans (Thorpe and Crompton, 2009; Ashbury et al., 2015; Spehar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and represents established knowledge.

claim: ENSO events may impact orangutan energy balance, reproduction, and social organization through the inducement of mast-fruiting.
source: Supra-annual ENSO events may also impact orangutan energy balance, reproduction, and social organization through the inducement of mast-fruiting, or dramatic seed production events in dipterocarp forests (Knott, 1998; Curran et al., 1999; Marshall et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Climate fluctuations over the past several hundred years have been documented in coral isotopes and tree-ring analyses.
source: Such climate fluctuations over the past several hundred years have been documented in coral isotopes and tree-ring analyses, revealing especially marked changes during the past few decades (Cole et al., 1993; Stahle et al., 1998; Hughen et al., 1999; Urban et al., 2000; Tudhope et al., 2001; Pumijumnong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Oxygen isotopes in fossil corals from seven periods during the last 130,000 years suggest that ENSO activity in the western Pacific over that time was comparable to modern records.
source: For example, oxygen isotopes in fossil corals from seven periods during the last 130,000 years suggest that ENSO activity in the western Pacific over that time was comparable to modern records, although there was variation in the intensity of such activity at different timepoints (Tudhope et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Oxygen isotope values (δ18O) in water vary with latitude, altitude, temperature, and precipitation cycles.
source: Oxygen isotope values (δ18O) in water vary with latitude, altitude, temperature, and precipitation cycles, and are also impacted by precipitation sources.
evidence: This represents established scientific knowledge in isotope geochemistry.

claim: In tropical regions the primary determinant of rainfall isotope compositions is rainfall amount.
source: In tropical regions the primary determinant of rainfall isotope compositions is rainfall amount (Dansgaard, 1964; Rozanski et al., 1993; Belgaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: During wet seasons, rainfall δ18O values are relatively low.
source: During wet seasons, rainfall δ18O values are relatively low, while the opposite pattern is evident in periods with less rain, although other meteorological factors can influence isotope values as well (Belgaman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: During dry seasons, rainfall δ18O values are relatively high.
source: During wet seasons, rainfall δ18O values are relatively low, while the opposite pattern is evident in periods with less rain, although other meteorological factors can influence isotope values as well (Belgaman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Unlike bone, teeth do not remodel during life.
source: Unlike bone, teeth do not remodel during life, and the phosphate component of the enamel mineral (hydroxyapatite) is especially resistant to modification after burial (reviewed in Smith et al., 2018a; Pederzani and Britton, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and represents established knowledge.

claim: The phosphate component of the enamel mineral (hydroxyapatite) is especially resistant to modification after burial.
source: Unlike bone, teeth do not remodel during life, and the phosphate component of the enamel mineral (hydroxyapatite) is especially resistant to modification after burial (reviewed in Smith et al., 2018a; Pederzani and Britton, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: δ18O values in tooth enamel are closely related to local water oxygen isotope compositions.
source: It is well established that δ18O values in tooth enamel are closely related to local water oxygen isotope compositions (reviewed in Green et al., 2018; Green et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: For teeth that form after birth and during periods of milk consumption, δ18O values are expected to be higher, as a result of infant evaporative water loss while consuming 18O-enriched mother's milk.
source: For teeth that form after birth and during periods of milk consumption, δ18O values are expected to be higher, as a result of infant evaporative water loss while consuming 18O-enriched mother's milk (Bryant et al., 1996; Wright and Schwarcz, 1999; Britton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Studies of large-bodied mammals report that milk δ18O values are elevated by ~1–6‰ relative to local drinking water δ18O.
source: Studies of large-bodied mammals report that milk δ18O values are elevated by ~1–6‰ relative to local drinking water δ18O (Kornexl et al., 1997; Lin et al., 2006; Chesson et al., 2010; Green et al., 2018; but see Cherney et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The urine of breast-fed infants showed isotopic enrichment of 1–3‰ compared to infants who were fed formula prepared from sterile local tap water.
source: The urine of infants who were breast-fed showed isotopic enrichment of 1–3‰ compared to infants who were fed formula prepared from sterile local tap water.
evidence: This is based on a study of 44 British infants mentioned in the text.

claim: Two studies of δ18O values in the dentitions of modern sheep, horses, and zebras reported higher bulk values (~1–2‰) in five molars (M1) compared to the rest of the permanent dentition.
source: Two studies of δ18O values in the dentitions of modern sheep, horses, and zebras reported higher bulk values (~1–2‰) in five molars (M1) compared to the rest of the permanent dentition (Bryant et al., 1996; Fricke and O'Neil, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Fricke and O'Neil, 1996, suggested that M1s are unlikely to reflect the values of local meteoric water due to the influence of maternal inputs in utero and through lactation.
source: This led Fricke and O'Neil, 1996, to suggest that M1s are unlikely to reflect the values of local meteoric water due to the influence of maternal inputs in utero and through lactation.
evidence: This is a citation to a published suggestion.

claim: Near-weekly δ18O values over the first 2.75 years of life in a Neanderthal M1 measured with SHRIMP SI showed clear annual trends and maximum δ18O values corresponding to a period after nursing has ceased.
source: However, near-weekly δ18O values over the first 2.75 years of life in a Neanderthal M1 measured with SHRIMP SI showed clear annual trends and maximum δ18O values corresponding to a period after nursing has ceased (Smith et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Comparisons of δ18O values during the first, second, and third years of life in five modern orangutan first molars (M1) do not show consistently elevated values during their first year.
source: Comparisons of δ18O values during the first, second, and third years of life in five modern orangutan first molars (M1) do not show consistently elevated values during their first year (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mean yearly δ18O values in the first year are elevated by only 0.3‰ compared to the second year in five modern orangutan first molars.
source: Mean yearly δ18O values in the first year are elevated by only 0.3‰ compared to the second year.
evidence: This is based on data analysis of modern orangutan teeth.

claim: Three of the five M1s showed first year δ18O values higher than second year values (p≤0.05).
source: While three of the five M1s showed first year δ18O values higher than second year values (p≤0.05), only two individuals showed mean values that were ~1–2‰ higher during year 1; one individual showed no difference from the first to the second year, and one individual showed lower values during the first year than during the second year (p≤0.05) (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data presented in Table 3.

claim: Only two individuals showed mean values that were ~1–2‰ higher during year 1 compared to year 2.
source: While three of the five M1s showed first year δ18O values higher than second year values (p≤0.05), only two individuals showed mean values that were ~1–2‰ higher during year 1; one individual showed no difference from the first to the second year, and one individual showed lower values during the first year than during the second year (p≤0.05) (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Comparisons across serial molars in four modern orangutans show no consistent trend of elevated δ18O values in M1s relative to successive molars.
source: Comparisons across serial molars in four modern orangutans show no consistent trend of elevated δ18O values in M1s relative to successive molars (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Values from the three Bornean individuals ranged from 12.7‰ to 20.0‰ (n=955 near weekly measurements).
source: Values from the three Bornean individuals ranged from 12.7‰ to 20.0‰ (n=955 near weekly measurements), while the three Sumatran individuals ranged from 11.3‰ to 20.6‰ (n=1061 measurements).
evidence: This is based on data measurements from modern orangutan teeth.

claim: Values from the three Sumatran individuals ranged from 11.3‰ to 20.6‰ (n=1061 measurements).
source: Values from the three Bornean individuals ranged from 12.7‰ to 20.0‰ (n=955 near weekly measurements), while the three Sumatran individuals ranged from 11.3‰ to 20.6‰ (n=1061 measurements).
evidence: This is based on data measurements from modern orangutan teeth.

claim: Three of the six Bornean molars were aperiodic (statistical power of 0.1 or less).
source: Comparisons of periodic trends via spectral power distribution analysis revealed more consistent bimodal patterns in the Sumatran individuals; three of the six Bornean molars were aperiodic (statistical power of 0.1 or less), while all six of the Sumatran molars revealed annual or semiannual cycles with greater power (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is based on spectral power distribution analysis of the data.

claim: All six of the Sumatran molars revealed annual or semiannual cycles with greater power.
source: Comparisons of periodic trends via spectral power distribution analysis revealed more consistent bimodal patterns in the Sumatran individuals; three of the six Bornean molars were aperiodic (statistical power of 0.1 or less), while all six of the Sumatran molars revealed annual or semiannual cycles with greater power (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is based on spectral power distribution analysis of the data.

claim: Rapid oxygen isotopic shifts on the order of ~6–8‰ are evident in the single Bornean and Sumatran individuals with δ18O measurements spanning M1 to M3.
source: Rapid oxygen isotopic shifts on the order of ~6–8‰ are evident in the single Bornean and Sumatran individuals with δ18O measurements spanning M1 to M3, which may represent one or more supra-annual ENSO events captured during the ~9–11 years these molars were forming.
evidence: This is based on data analysis and inference about ENSO events.

claim: Rapid oxygen isotopic shifts of ~6–8‰ may represent one or more supra-annual ENSO events captured during the ~9–11 years these molars were forming.
source: Rapid oxygen isotopic shifts on the order of ~6–8‰ are evident in the single Bornean and Sumatran individuals with δ18O measurements spanning M1 to M3, which may represent one or more supra-annual ENSO events captured during the ~9–11 years these molars were forming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and knowledge of ENSO events.

claim: Concurrently forming teeth (molar specimens 11594.12 and 11595.105) from same individual at Lida Ajer, Sumatra, are nearly isotopically identical.
source: Concurrently forming teeth (molar specimens 11594.12 and 11595.105) from same individual at Lida Ajer, Sumatra, are nearly isotopically identical; δ18O values range from 15.1‰ to 19.9‰ and 15.7‰ to 20.0‰, respectively, supporting the biogenic fidelity of these records.
evidence: This is based on data measurements from fossil teeth and supports the reliability of the isotopic records.

claim: The δ18O values of two individuals from the nearby Sibrambang site (15.3–20.4‰, 14.7–20.8‰) are very similar to those of the Lida Ajer individual.
source: The δ18O values of two individuals from the nearby Sibrambang site (15.3–20.4‰, 14.7–20.8‰) are very similar to those of the Lida Ajer individual.
evidence: This is based on data measurements from fossil teeth.

claim: Sumatran fossils all fall at the upper end of the range of modern Sumatran orangutans.
source: These Sumatran fossils all fall at the upper end of the range of modern Sumatran orangutans (Figure 4), and reveal approximately annual δ18O periodicities (0.9–1.3 years), as well as strong bimodal distribution patterns in one instance (11565.162).
evidence: This is based on comparison of fossil and modern data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sumatran fossil orangutans reveal approximately annual δ18O periodicities (0.9–1.3 years).
source: These Sumatran fossils all fall at the upper end of the range of modern Sumatran orangutans (Figure 4), and reveal approximately annual δ18O periodicities (0.9–1.3 years), as well as strong bimodal distribution patterns in one instance (11565.162).
evidence: This is based on data analysis of fossil teeth.

claim: δ18O values in the tooth from grid US/22 ranged from 15.9‰ to 24.8‰ and yielded an annual periodicity (1.0 years).
source: The two fossils from the Niah Caves were excavated from different regions and stratigraphic depths; δ18O values in the tooth from grid US/22 ranged from 15.9‰ to 24.8‰ and, unlike the three modern Bornean individuals, yielded an annual periodicity (1.0 years).
evidence: This is based on data measurements and analysis from a fossil tooth.

claim: The δ18O in the tooth from grid Y/F4 ranged from 14.2‰ to 22.9‰ and showed a stronger bimodal trend than an annual one.
source: The δ18O in the tooth from grid Y/F4 ranged from 14.2‰ to 22.9‰ and showed a stronger bimodal trend than an annual one, although its short formation time may have prohibited identification of longer trends.
evidence: This is based on data measurements and analysis from a fossil tooth.

claim: The range of values from the two Niah Caves fossil molars (14.2–24.8‰) markedly exceeds the range of modern Bornean orangutans (12.7–20.0‰).
source: The range of values from these two fossil molars (14.2–24.8‰) markedly exceeds the range of modern Bornean orangutans (12.7–20.0‰) (Figure 4), with the mean δ18O value at least 2‰ heavier.
evidence: This is based on comparison of fossil and modern data.

claim: The mean δ18O value of Niah Caves fossil molars is at least 2‰ heavier than modern Bornean orangutans.
source: The range of values from these two fossil molars (14.2–24.8‰) markedly exceeds the range of modern Bornean orangutans (12.7–20.0‰) (Figure 4), with the mean δ18O value at least 2‰ heavier.
evidence: This is based on comparison of fossil and modern data.

claim: The difference in δ18O values between Niah Caves fossils and modern Bornean orangutans suggests possibly drier conditions with greater seasonality during fossil molar formation.
source: This suggests possibly drier conditions with greater seasonality during fossil molar formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in δ18O data.

claim: The six fossil teeth have very low uranium concentrations in their enamel (<0.5 ppm), regardless of their origin.
source: The six fossil teeth have very low uranium concentrations in their enamel (<0.5 ppm), regardless of their origin (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on uranium concentration measurements.

claim: The enamel uranium values are very close to the detection limit of the Nu Plasma II MC-ICP-MS, and thus are not useful for estimating minimum ages.
source: These enamel values are very close to the detection limit of the Nu Plasma II MC-ICP-MS, and thus are not useful for estimating minimum ages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured uranium concentrations and instrument capabilities.

claim: The dentine of Lida Ajer specimen 11595.105 shows a spatial gradient of increasing uranium concentration from ~41 to 66 ppm.
source: The dentine of Lida Ajer specimen 11595.105 shows a spatial gradient of increasing uranium concentration from ~41 to 66 ppm, and decreasing age estimates from ~51 to 40 ka (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on uranium concentration measurements in dentine.

claim: Lida Ajer specimen 11595.105 has a minimum age of ~40 ka.
source: Spot DE10, positioned near the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), is less likely to be impacted (Appendix 1—figure 3), and is thus assumed to provide the most reliable minimum age for the tooth, ~40 ka.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis and inference about which measurement is most reliable.

claim: Lida Ajer specimen 11594.12 has a minimum age of 33 ka.
source: No evidence for a recent overprint is observed, supporting a minimum age of 33 ka. In summary, this individual's age is at least 33 ka, and possibly >40 ka.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: Sibrambang specimen 11565.162 has a minimum age of 60 ka.
source: This might result from a slight uranium leaching overprint; a minimum age of 60 ka is likely for this tooth.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis and inference about uranium leaching.

claim: Sibrambang specimen 11564.5 has a minimum age of 70.3±5.5 ka (2σ).
source: An average dentine U-series age of 70.3±5.5 ka (2σ) may be regarded as a minimum age for the fossil, which is broadly consistent with the single age estimate obtained from the enamel (64 ka).
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: The two teeth from Sibrambang yield U-series apparent ages of ~60–70 ka.
source: In summary, the two teeth from Sibrambang yield U-series apparent ages of ~60–70 ka.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: The Niah Caves specimen from grid Y/F4 has an average dentine U-series minimum age of 7.6±1.3 ka.
source: The average dentine U-series minimum age is 7.6±1.3 ka.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: The Niah Cave specimen from grid US/22 has an average dentine U-series age of 8.8±3.0 ka.
source: The average dentine U-series age is 8.8±3.0 ka.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: The two teeth from Niah Cave yield consistent apparent ages of ~8–9 ka, which should be regarded as a minimum age constraint for the fossils.
source: In summary, the two teeth from Niah Cave yield consistent apparent ages of ~8–9 ka, which should be regarded as a minimum age constraint for the fossils.
evidence: This is based on U-series dating analysis.

claim: Five modern orangutans show only minor and inconsistently elevated δ18O values during the first year of life when compared to the subsequent year.
source: We find that five modern orangutans show only minor and inconsistently elevated δ18O values during the first year of life when compared to the subsequent year.
evidence: This is based on data analysis of modern orangutan teeth.

claim: The data do not support the hypothesis that primate infants have markedly elevated body water δ18O values during exclusive nursing.
source: These data do not support the hypothesis that primate infants have markedly elevated body water δ18O values during exclusive nursing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis of orangutan teeth.

claim: Data from the majority of 12 human M1s studied by Vaiglova et al., 2024, reveal maximum δ18O values after the first year of tooth formation.
source: Data from the majority of 12 human M1s studied by Vaiglova et al., 2024, similarly reveal maximum δ18O values after the first year of tooth formation, well beyond the duration of exclusive milk intake.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Orangutan infants rely exclusively on maternal milk during their first year of life.
source: Orangutan infants rely exclusively on maternal milk during their first year of life, supplementing this with solid foods in the second year, which are increased until suckling ceases prior to 9 years of age (van Noordwijk et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Orangutan suckling ceases prior to 9 years of age.
source: Orangutan infants rely exclusively on maternal milk during their first year of life, supplementing this with solid foods in the second year, which are increased until suckling ceases prior to 9 years of age (van Noordwijk et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The two Bornean juveniles from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/48, ZSM 1981/87) reflect the environmental conditions of the late 1880s and early 1890s in Skalau.
source: The two Bornean juveniles from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/48, ZSM 1981/87) reflect the environmental conditions of the late 1880s and early 1890s in Skalau—a region where orangutans might now be locally extinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collection dates and location of the specimens.

claim: Orangutans might now be locally extinct in Skalau.
source: The two Bornean juveniles from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/48, ZSM 1981/87) reflect the environmental conditions of the late 1880s and early 1890s in Skalau—a region where orangutans might now be locally extinct.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about current orangutan distribution.

claim: The teeth from the two Sumatran individuals from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/246, ZSM 1981/248) were collected prior to 1939 in northern Aceh.
source: Similarly, the teeth from the two Sumatran individuals from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/246, ZSM 1981/248) were collected prior to 1939 in northern Aceh, from where orangutans also have since disappeared (Spehar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on collection records.

claim: Orangutans have since disappeared from northern Aceh.
source: Similarly, the teeth from the two Sumatran individuals from the Munich collection (ZSM 1981/246, ZSM 1981/248) were collected prior to 1939 in northern Aceh, from where orangutans also have since disappeared (Spehar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Orangutans obtain the majority of their body water from plants.
source: Another potential source of isotopic variability derives from dietary variation, as orangutans obtain the majority of their body water from plants (Mackinnon, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Plant oxygen isotope compositions can be stratified within tropical forest canopies.
source: Plant oxygen isotope compositions can be stratified within tropical forest canopies (da Silveira et al., 1989; Roberts et al., 2017; Lowry et al., 2021)—potentially leading to offset values among various animals, including primates, that consume different resources in the same forest (Krigbaum et al., 2013; Nelson, 2013; Fannin and Scott McGraw, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Bornean and Sumatran orangutans obtain 95% of their food from the middle and upper levels of the canopy.
source: Mackinnon, 1974, reported that Bornean and Sumatran orangutans obtain 95% of their food from the middle and upper levels of the canopy, where preferred foods are most abundant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Orangutan δ18O values are quite similar to the δ18O values from five humans from Flores, Indonesia (14.8–21.0‰) dated at ~2.2–3.0 ka.
source: Orangutan δ18O values are also quite similar to the δ18O values from five humans from Flores, Indonesia (14.8–21.0‰) dated at ~2.2–3.0 ka (Vaiglova et al., 2024).
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from a cited study.

claim: The similarity between orangutan and human δ18O values suggests that their enamel δ18O values are predominantly influenced by regional precipitation.
source: This is remarkable given the major dietary differences between frugivorous orangutans and omnivorous coastal-dwelling humans, and suggests that their enamel δ18O values are predominantly influenced by regional precipitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of orangutan and human data.

claim: Dating studies at Lida Ajer have established the presence of the oldest human remains in insular Southeast Asia, ~63–73 ka.
source: Dating studies at Lida Ajer have established the presence of the oldest human remains in insular Southeast Asia, ~63–73 ka (Westaway et al., 2017), and a broad survey of the cave has reconfirmed an age of MIS 4 (59–76 ka) for the mammalian fauna (Louys et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: A broad survey of Lida Ajer cave has reconfirmed an age of MIS 4 (59–76 ka) for the mammalian fauna.
source: Dating studies at Lida Ajer have established the presence of the oldest human remains in insular Southeast Asia, ~63–73 ka (Westaway et al., 2017), and a broad survey of the cave has reconfirmed an age of MIS 4 (59–76 ka) for the mammalian fauna (Louys et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The Sumatran Sibrambang Cave has been regarded as roughly contemporaneous to Lida Ajer given broad faunal similarities.
source: The Sumatran Sibrambang Cave has been regarded as roughly contemporaneous to Lida Ajer given broad faunal similarities (de Vos, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Analysis of δ18O values in Sumatran orangutan fossil molars reveals a close similarity across sites and with modern Sumatran individuals.
source: Our analysis of δ18O values in Sumatran orangutan fossil molars reveals a close similarity across sites and with modern Sumatran individuals, although the fossil compositions fall at the upper end of the modern range.
evidence: This is based on comparison of fossil and modern δ18O data.

claim: The fossil compositions fall at the upper end of the modern range, which may indicate a slightly dryer and less variable climate during the late Pleistocene.
source: Our analysis of δ18O values in Sumatran orangutan fossil molars reveals a close similarity across sites and with modern Sumatran individuals, although the fossil compositions fall at the upper end of the modern range. This may indicate a slightly dryer and less variable climate during the late Pleistocene; elevated tooth δ18O values are also indicative of elevated values in hydrological systems globally, resulting from increased ice volumes in glaciers and at the poles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed δ18O data and knowledge of isotope systematics.

claim: The higher δ18O values in the Niah Cave orangutans are possibly indicative of reduced rainfall when compared to recent conditions.
source: Given the similar offsets in δ18O values between modern baboons living in Ugandan forests and the Ethiopian rift region (Green et al., 2022) and modern and prehistoric Bornean orangutans, we regard the higher δ18O values in the Niah Cave orangutans as possibly indicative of reduced rainfall when compared to recent conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with other primate studies and the observed δ18O data.

claim: The higher δ18O values in Niah Cave orangutans are consistent with paleoclimate reconstructions for Borneo and Flores during the late Pleistocene and early Holocene.
source: This is consistent with paleoclimate reconstructions for Borneo and Flores during the late Pleistocene and early Holocene (Griffiths et al., 2009; Buckingham et al., 2022), when the environment around the Niah Caves is believed to have been a drier, more open seasonal forest (Harrison, 1996; Hunt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Dental tissues are known to behave as open systems for U-series elements.
